newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinian lawmakers assail PLO corruption.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian lawmakers assail PLO corruption.

text.p: Palestinian lawmakers accused members of Yasser Arafat's self-rule administration on Wednesday of corruption and misuse of taxpayer's money in a stormy session of parliament.
What was slated to be a debate on the long overdue 1997 budget proposal turned into a sharp exchange between irate legislators elected more than a year ago and members of the Palestinian Authority.

"The council's economic committee found that tax-payer's money has been misused," said legislator Saad al-Krunz, reading from a report on the budget prepared by the Council's economic committee which he chairs.
Legislators complained the Palestinian Authority had appointed officials based on favouritism rather than their qualifications and charged that government offices were crowded with useless employees.
Others said the Authority was subsidising two or more homes for Palestinian ministers.

"We have information that some ministers have more than one house, one in the West Bank and another in Gaza...paid by the Authority," said legislator Jamileh Saidam. She was jeered by some ministers who explained they had jobs in both areas.
Finance Minister Mohammed al-Nashashibi conceded that reforms were necessary but pointed a finger at legislators, saing some of them were guilty of corruption.
He rejected demands for greater supervision of the Authority's spending.
"Our auditing committee is active and we have transparency and we are making great efforts to reduce expenses in order to reduce the $52 million budget deficit," he told legislators.
The Legislative Council was due to discuss the Palestinian Authority's draft law of the $866 million 1997 budget, submitted to lawmakers six months late.
This is the first time since Palestinian President Arafat set up his self-rule administration in parts of the West Bank and Gaza in 1994 that a budget proposal is presented to parliament.
Legislators had sharply criticised the Authority for failing to submit the budget on time, some threatening to bring down the government.
Palestinians frequently complain about corruption in official circles and oppressive measures by at least seven branches of PLO police and security.
Others charge that while unemployment is skyrocketing and economic conditions are deteriorating, senior PLO officials were building huge homes and owned several late-model cars.
"Have mercy on our people for the chaos that engulfs our institutions," said legislator Ahmed al-Batsh.
